function.name: calculate_electric_current
function.description: Calculate the electric current through a conductor given voltage and resistance. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

voltage.description: The voltage across the conductor in Volts. This is a float type value.

resistance.description: The resistance of the conductor in Ohms. This is a float type value.

conductance.description: The conductance of the conductor in Siemens. Optional if resistance is provided. Default: 0.3 This is a float type value.

message.content:
Electricity wasn’t “discovered” by a single individual—instead it was gradually uncovered by many scientists and thinkers over millennia. Here’s a quick timeline highlighting some of the most influential contributors:

| Time | Key Figure(s) | Contribution |
|------|---------------|--------------|
| **c. 600 BCE** | *Thales of Miletus* | First recorded observation of static electricity using amber (“electrum”). |
| **17th century** | *William Gilbert* (1544‑1603) | Distinguished between magnetism and electrostatics; coined the word *electric* from Greek *elektron*. Published *De Magnete*, laying groundwork for electrical science. |
| **Late 1600s – early 1700s** | *Otto von Guericke*, *Stephen Gray*, *Charles François de Cisternay du Fay* | Explored conduction vs insulation, identified positive/negative charges, and studied charge separation. |
| **1752** | *Benjamin Franklin* | Conducted famous kite experiment proving lightning is electrical discharge; introduced concepts of positive & negative charge, and developed the idea of conservation of charge. |
| **1800** | *Alessandro Volta* | Invented the voltaic pile (the first chemical battery), demonstrating continuous direct current generation. |
| **1821** | *Michael Faraday* | Discovered electromagnetic induction—changing magnetic fields produce electric currents. |
| **1831** | *James Clerk Maxwell* | Unified electromagnetism into four equations describing how changing electric and magnetic fields generate each other. |

These pioneers—and countless others before and after them—collectively built our modern understanding of electricity. So while no single person “discovered” electricity outright, its study evolved through cumulative insights spanning ancient philosophy to contemporary physics.
